primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Abbott said Mar 18 FDA granted EUA for molecular COVID-19 test — would ship 150,000 tests immediately. Not company-specific bad news. Broad de-risking move
secondary_factors: Healthcare outperformed many sectors during March 2020 crash overall but that relative strength did not prevent single-day liquidation on March 23
store_description: Abbott actually had favorable COVID-testing news in the lookback window including EUA and shipment plans for 150,000 molecular tests so the 7.6% drop does not line up with a negative company catalyst. The more likely story is that investors sold liquid large-cap names indiscriminately as the S&P 500 hit its closing low.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mar 19 Accenture cut full-year revenue growth forecast to 3-6% from 6-8% because of coronavirus disruption. Guidance reset likely remained clearest reason for Mar 23 decline
secondary_factors: On March 23 risk assets were still under pressure from shutdown-driven recession scare and stalled fiscal package talks
store_description: Accenture had a concrete stock-specific negative development: management reduced expected FY revenue growth by 200 basis points at both ends to 3-6% from 6-8% citing the pandemic. That guidance reset likely remained the clearest reason for the stock 4.2% decline on March 23.

primary_cause: No strong company-specific negative Mar 20-22. REIT and real-estate sector liquidation during Mar 23 low. Real-estate equities among hardest-hit groups
secondary_factors: Funding and liquidity concerns across income vehicles. Forced selling across REITs even where tower cash flows were sturdier than retail or office
store_description: AMT 8.3% drop looks much more like a sector and liquidity event than a reaction to a specific corporate announcement. In the March 2020 crash real-estate stocks were among the weakest cohorts and March 23 was still dominated by indiscriminate selling pressure despite the Fed support measures.

primary_cause: No major company-specific Mar 20-23 AXP headline. Market heavily repricing card issuers for collapse in travel and higher consumer credit losses. Fed Mar 23 facilities included support for consumer-credit-linked ABS
secondary_factors: Marketwide selloff. Consumer-finance sensitivity to sudden shutdown in airlines hotels restaurants and T&E
store_description: AXP model had unusually high exposure to travel and entertainment spending so by March 23 investors were discounting both a sharp revenue hit and rising charge-offs even without a fresh company release. The 7.0% fall fits the broader consumer-credit repricing.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. Mar 15 biggest U.S. banks including BofA said would halt stock buybacks. Bank-sector stress driven by recession fears near-zero rates worsening credit expectations. Buyback suspension reinforcing how serious conditions had become
secondary_factors: Flattening rates. Pressure on net interest income. Fears over consumer and commercial defaults. Fed encouraging banks to use capital and liquidity buffers
store_description: BAC 8.1% drop was most likely driven by the bank group worsening earnings outlook rather than a BAC-only event. The prior-week decision by large banks to suspend buybacks signaled capital preservation while the March 23 environment was still pricing in severe loan losses and margin compression.

primary_cause: BNY Mellon among large banks that suspended buybacks Mar 15. Extreme stress in Treasury repo and funding markets where BNY Mellon directly exposed as major plumbing provider. Financial-system stress and bank-sector derating
secondary_factors: Buyback suspension. Custody and market-sensitive fee concerns. Extraordinary volume and dislocation in core funding markets
store_description: BK 5.4% decline fits a custody-bank version of the March bank selloff: investors were nervous about fee income systemic stress and the signal sent by the industrywide suspension of buybacks. The background stress in repo and Treasury clearing markets made the sector look riskier.

primary_cause: No material BlackRock-specific negative Mar 20-22. ETFs and credit markets under acute stress. Major discounts opening between ETF prices and NAVs. Asset-manager and ETF ecosystem stress during March credit and liquidity dislocation
secondary_factors: Lower AUM from market declines. Outflow fears. Pressure on credit ETFs before Fed facilities gained credibility
store_description: BLK 7.7% slide was probably not tied to a company announcement but to the broader panic in credit and ETF markets where BlackRock had high perceived exposure. In March 2020 discounts in parts of the ETF market and severe funding stress made asset managers especially vulnerable to de-rating.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mar 23 Bristol Myers said would delay starting new clinical trials for at least three weeks because of pandemic. Clinical-trial delay announcement
secondary_factors: General healthcare selling. Concern about slower launches enrollment and commercialization
store_description: BMY had a clean stock-specific catalyst: management paused the start of new clinical trials for at least three weeks directly signaling COVID-related pipeline disruption. That made the stock 4.1% decline look more company-driven than many other names on the list.

primary_cause: Citi said Mar 15 joining other large U.S. banks in suspending stock repurchases. Already announced customer relief steps. Bank-sector recession and credit-loss fears with buyback suspension as confirming signal
secondary_factors: Rates pressure. Global credit exposure. Fiscal-stimulus uncertainty on March 23
store_description: Citi 7.0% decline fits the same pattern as BAC and JPM: the market was pricing a deep recession higher loan losses and weaker capital returns. The March 15 buyback suspension was not the sole cause but it reinforced the sector defensive posture.

primary_cause: No Mar 20-23 Reuters item before drop. Later that week Caterpillar withdrew guidance and suspended some operations. Cyclical industrial recession fears tied to shutdowns and capital-spending retrenchment
secondary_factors: Exposure to construction mining energy and dealer financing all being marked down sharply in late March
store_description: CAT 3.8% decline appears driven mainly by the market anticipating a collapse in equipment demand rather than by a same-day corporate headline. The fact that Caterpillar withdrew its 2020 outlook and suspended operations just three days later on March 26 supports that investors were already discounting severe pandemic damage.

primary_cause: No Berkshire-specific negative Mar 20-22. Large public-equity portfolio including banks airlines cyclical businesses getting hit hard. Look-through exposure to broader market especially financials and economically sensitive holdings
secondary_factors: Investor concern about operating subsidiaries tied to transport manufacturing retail and insurance in shutdown economy
store_description: BRK-B 4.7% fall was most likely a portfolio and economic-exposure story not a Berkshire-only headline. By mid-March investors were already estimating tens of billions of dollars of mark-to-market damage to Berkshire listed holdings while recession risk threatened many of its operating businesses.

primary_cause: Oil demand collapsing because of COVID. Reuters Feb reported Conoco expected demand growth to slow. Industry rolling out steep spending cuts — COP cut operating spending by ~$700M ~10%. Oil demand destruction plus Saudi-Russia price war
secondary_factors: Anticipation of capex and opex cuts. Lower realized prices. Recession fears. Crude had collapsed to roughly $22.43 WTI and $26.98 Brent
store_description: COP 8.5% drop lines up with the late-March oil panic when crude had collapsed. Investors were repricing the whole upstream complex for a demand shock and COP was already publicly warning that coronavirus would slow demand growth.

primary_cause: Later disclosed da Vinci procedures in last half of March 2020 fell to roughly 65% of earlier Q1 weekly rate. Elective surgery shutdown risk. Hospital resource diversion to COVID care
secondary_factors: Expected delays in robot placements and utilization
store_description: Even without a March 20-23 press release ISRG was highly exposed to the sudden cancellation of elective procedures which investors were already beginning to price aggressively by March 23. Later disclosures showing procedure activity falling to about 65% of earlier-quarter levels support that the market was correctly anticipating a sharp utilization shock.

primary_cause: Mar 20 Treasury/IRS moved U.S. tax filing deadline from Apr 15 to Jul 15. Intuit later disclosed extension affected usage timing across tax products. Tax-season revenue timing disruption from filing extension
secondary_factors: General software multiple compression during March 23 panic though software as a sector held up relatively better over the full crash
store_description: INTU 3.5% fall likely reflected investor concern that moving the deadline to July 15 would shift or delay core TurboTax activity and near-term monetization. That company-specific timing issue seems more relevant than a generic market explanation here.

primary_cause: No strong COF-specific Mar 20-23 headline. Market sharply repricing monoline and card-heavy lenders for unemployment charge-offs payment stress. Fed Mar 23 actions specifically targeted consumer-credit ABS markets. Consumer-credit loss fears
secondary_factors: Funding market strain. Recession expectations. Exposure to card balances and auto lending
store_description: COF 4.8% decline looks like a credit-cycle call rather than a company-news reaction. Investors were anticipating a rapid deterioration in household credit quality and consumer spending especially for lenders with heavier unsecured and subprime-adjacent exposure.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mar 23 GE said would cut aviation workforce by about 10% as travel collapse hit jet market. Stock fell to 28-year low. Aviation job-cut announcement and worsening aerospace outlook
secondary_factors: Liquidity concerns around GE cyclical businesses. Broader March 23 market low
store_description: GE had a direct negative catalyst on the day of the decline: aviation one of its most important businesses was cutting roughly 10% of its workforce as airline demand collapsed. That company-specific shock combined with GE already fragile turnaround story made the 6.3% drop more than just macro noise.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC. Mar 23 Reuters carried company disclosure that General Dynamics said its business could be negatively impacted by coronavirus outbreak. COVID-impact warning especially around Gulfstream and commercial exposure
secondary_factors: Defense names not immune to marketwide liquidation. Business-jet demand particularly vulnerable
store_description: GD 6.5% decline had a real stock-specific headline behind it: the company explicitly warned on March 23 that coronavirus could hurt business. Investors likely focused on Gulfstream sensitivity to the shutdown in travel and corporate activity.

primary_cause: No negative Honeywell-specific news Mar 20-23. Mar 10 had reaffirmed Q1 and full-year outlook. Industrial and aerospace recession fears not negative company news. Macro deterioration overwhelming earlier management reassurance
secondary_factors: Exposure to commercial aerospace building technologies and short-cycle industrial demand
store_description: Because the available pre-drop headline was positive rather than negative HON 7.7% move is best explained by investors sharply marking down industrial and aerospace earnings power as lockdowns spread. The stock was reacting to macro deterioration overwhelming earlier management reassurance.

primary_cause: No Duke-specific negative Mar 20-22. Utilities hit as investors sold anything liquid. Concerns about commercial and industrial electricity demand and financing conditions. Defensive-sector liquidation during Mar 23 panic
secondary_factors: Lower expected power demand from business shutdowns. Pressure on rate-sensitive sectors amid funding stress
store_description: DUK 6.2% drop looks mostly like indiscriminate selling in a market that was still searching for a bottom not a response to a Duke announcement. Utilities were relatively defensive fundamentally but on March 23 even many defensives were sold to raise cash.

primary_cause: STOCK-SPECIFIC context. JPMorgan said Mar 15 would stop buying back shares and use capital to lend to customers. Bank-sector credit-cycle fears with buyback halt reinforcing pressure. Margin pressure from emergency Fed easing
secondary_factors: Recession expectations. Delayed fiscal stimulus
store_description: JPM 5.4% decline fits the broader bank selloff but the March 15 buyback suspension mattered because it signaled management was prioritizing capital preservation and customer support over shareholder returns. Investors were simultaneously pricing weaker net interest income and a sharp rise in expected loan losses.
